title: How To Master Understanding Of Your AWS Bills and Tools You Can Use?
summary: Master your AWS bills with Cost Explorer, Budgets, and Trusted Advisor. Understand pricing structures and cost datasets to optimize cloud spending.
body_markdown:
## Introduction


AWS provides you with an unlimited amount of cloud and various services. Still, it does not change the fact that it can have spikes in your all-over cost if your AWS resources are not kept in check. A lot of focus is paid to understanding the various services like EC2, CloudWatch, etc. But there is little attention paid to how to read your AWS bills. I will explain how to read your AWS bills and the tools you can use to lower your overall bill.


> **2026 update — the fundamentals here (pricing model, cost datasets, and the core tools) are still accurate, but AWS has reorganized the billing console and added several important cost tools since 2020. Read the inline notes for what is new.**
>
>
> The pricing philosophy (pay as you go, pay less by using more, save when you reserve) and the cost datasets (unblended, amortized, blended, and the net variants) are unchanged and still correct — you can rely on those sections as written. What has moved on is the tooling: the Billing console has been split and renamed, **Savings Plans** have largely become the default commitment mechanism, and AWS shipped two free tools that did not exist when this was written — **Cost Optimization Hub** and **Cost Anomaly Detection** — that you should be using in 2026. Each tool section below carries a note bringing it current.


To view your current or past AWS bills, you must open the Bills pane in the Billing and Cost Management console. Then you must choose the month you want to view your bill from the drop-down menu.


> **2026 update — the console navigation has changed.** AWS reorganized this area into the **AWS Billing and Cost Management** console, and the cost-analysis features now live under a distinct **Cost Management** grouping (Cost Explorer, Budgets, Cost Optimization Hub, Cost Anomaly Detection, and Data Exports) separate from the pure billing/invoice pages. The concepts below are identical; only the menu layout differs, so if a screenshot or menu name here does not match what you see, look under “Billing and Cost Management” and its “Cost Management” section. As you are always charged on your usage basis, you must check your AWS bills often. AWS Bills are finalized at the beginning of each month, and after finalizing, you can download a PDF version of your bill and any tax invoices applicable to your bill.


### Pricing Structure


With the wide variety of services provided by Amazon Web Services, the prediction and management of costs for large deployments can be very complicated. AWS has a pricing structure based on three essential points. These are:


- Pay as you go
- Payless by using more
- Save when you reserve


I will explain each of these points for your better understanding.


### Pay as you go


AWS leases computing resources to turn capital expenses into operating expenses, and it lets its users pay for them hourly.


You should leverage “[Pay as you go](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-on-demand-instances.html?ref=cloudanix.com) ” only for the workloads with unexpected peaks or scalability needs. This is because AWS has an On-Demand pricing scheme, which is expensive even for small workloads.


> **2026 update — “pay as you go” now extends well beyond hourly EC2, and per-second and serverless billing change the calculus.** The principle still holds, but two things have evolved. First, many services (including EC2 for Linux, and EBS) bill **per second** with a small minimum, not just per hour, so short-lived workloads are cheaper than the “hourly” framing implies. Second, **serverless options** — Lambda (per-request and per-millisecond), Fargate (per-second for containers), and on-demand modes for databases like DynamoDB and Aurora Serverless v2 — let you pay only for actual execution with zero idle cost. For genuinely spiky or infrequent workloads in 2026, serverless is often cheaper than keeping right-sized on-demand instances running, so evaluate it before defaulting to always-on compute.


### Pay less by using more


You are discounted on your total cost when you use specific service features and spend more than $500,000 on AWS upfront.


You establish yourself in the Amazon ecosystem when you increase your usage of AWS. You must balance your desire for discounts with the need to maintain a healthy, multi-cloud strategy.


> **2026 update — volume and tiered discounts still apply, but the bigger lever most teams miss is eliminating waste before committing to more spend.** The advice to balance discounts against lock-in is sound. Add one modern principle: do not commit to higher usage (or buy Savings Plans) on top of an unoptimized environment, or you simply lock in waste. The right order in 2026 is **rightsize and remove idle resources first** (using Compute Optimizer and Cost Optimization Hub), **then** commit to Savings Plans on the genuinely needed baseline. Also note that data transfer — especially cross-Region and internet egress — is a frequently overlooked line item; using VPC endpoints and keeping traffic in-Region can cut it materially, and it rarely shows up in “reserve to save” thinking.


### Save when you reserve


Amazon EC2 is the basis for most AWS, and it provides discounts of around 30% to 50% on AWS bills if you reserve instances in advance. (approximately 1-3 years in advance)


You must consider the workload on-premises before purchasing reserved instances. It will be cheaper if you use the same effect unless there is a need for the flexibility provided by the cloud.


> **2026 update — for most workloads, Savings Plans have replaced Reserved Instances as the commitment of choice.** Reserved Instances (RIs) still exist and the discount range above is broadly right, but AWS introduced **Savings Plans** , which give similar discounts (up to roughly 66–72% versus on-demand for a 1- or 3-year commitment) in exchange for a commitment to a steady dollar-per-hour spend, rather than to a specific instance type. The big advantage is flexibility: **Compute Savings Plans** automatically apply across EC2 instance families, Regions, operating systems, and even AWS Fargate and Lambda, so you keep the discount when you change instance types — something classic RIs do not allow. In 2026 the common pattern is: cover your stable baseline with Compute Savings Plans, use on-demand for spiky workloads, and use **Spot Instances** (up to ~90% off) for fault-tolerant or batch work. Another modern option worth knowing: **Graviton** (AWS’s Arm-based processors) often cuts costs a further 20% or so at better price-performance, and migrating to it is one of the top recommendations AWS’s own tools now surface.


### Ways in which AWS bills show your cost structure


AWS tailors its cost in a well-structured manner and provides several cost datasets to understand your AWS usage better. AWS Billing and Cost Management offer the following datasets for better cost management of users. These include:


1. Unblended costs
2. Amortized costs
3. Blended costs
4. Net unblended costs
5. Net amortized costs


I will explain the above datasets briefly to give you a rough idea of how AWS provides a well-structured cost.


### Unblended costs


This is vastly used by most of the AWS users and is presented on the Bills page. It is the default option for analyzing costs using AWS Cost Explorer. It is also the default option for setting custom budgets in AWS Budgets. This represents the usage costs charged to you on a cash basis of accounting. For most users, this is the only dataset they need.


### Amortized costs


When Unblended costs make little sense, Amortized costs come into the picture. It shows the costs on a rather accrual basis than a cash basis. This cost dataset is most useful for those who have purchased AWS Reservations such as Amazon EC2 Reserved Instances. If you are using unblended costs as your cost dataset, you might encounter a spike if recurring fees are charged on the first day of a month since savings plans and Reservations often have upfront or recurring monthly fees associated with them. Amortized costs help distribute these recurring costs evenly across the month. If you seek to gain insight into the effective daily costs associated with your reservation portfolio, amortized cost datasets are potent tools.


### Blended costs


Making sense of spend across many linked accounts is the same challenge as making sense of security across them, and a single[platform](https://www.cloudanix.com/platform) view helps on both fronts — as one team found when it moved[from tool sprawl to a single dashboard for ecommerce cloud security](https://www.cloudanix.com/use-cases/from-tool-sprawl-to-single-dashboard-ecommerce-cloud-security) and as seen in[securing multi-account AWS without a landing zone or Control Tower](https://www.cloudanix.com/use-cases/securing-multi-account-aws-without-a-landing-zone-or-control-tower) .


Users who want to merge their billing under a single paying account can focus on this unit. The way these are calculated makes it unlikely for people to use them. In this dataset, each account’s service usage is multiplied against a blended rate, which is an average rate of on-demand usage, Savings Plans, and Reservation related usage. Member accounts consume this in an organization for a specific service.


### Other costs dataset


In rare case scenarios, AWS users can take advantage of specialized discounts. The net unblended costs dataset gives the total cost after applying discounts. The net amortized costs dataset adds additional logic to amortize discount-related data besides your Savings Plans or Reservation associated charges.


One should choose cost datasets carefully. If you are using Savings Plans or Reservations, you will benefit from Amortized costs; otherwise, you must select the unblended cost dataset. If you are operating at scale or have a specific use case, you might go for other cost datasets like net unblended or net amortized datasets.


> **2026 update — this dataset guidance is still exactly right; here is how it plays out with modern commitment tools.** Because Savings Plans have become the common commitment mechanism (see the “Save when you reserve” note), the choice between unblended and amortized matters for almost every team that optimizes cost. If you buy an all-upfront or monthly Savings Plan, **unblended** costs will show a large charge on the purchase day and near-zero for the covered usage afterward — which makes daily trends look alarming and misleading. Switch your Cost Explorer and Budgets views to **amortized** costs so that commitment spreads evenly across the term and each day reflects the true effective cost of what you ran. A practical rule for 2026: use **amortized** for internal cost analysis and chargeback/showback (it reflects real economic cost per team), and use **unblended** only when you need to reconcile against the actual cash amounts on your invoice.


## AWS Cost Management Tools


AWS provides you with a set of tools for cost management and optimization, free of cost. These tools can save you a suitable amount of money on AWS, provided you familiarize yourself with these tools, use them to gain data, make decisions, create rules, and use automated actions.


**Some tools are, namely:**


1. [Billing and Cost Management Console](https://console.aws.amazon.com/billing/home/?ref=cloudanix.com)
2. [AWS Cost Explorer](https://aws.amazon.com/aws-cost-management/aws-cost-explorer/?ref=cloudanix.com)
3. [AWS Budgets](https://aws.amazon.com/aws-cost-management/aws-budgets/?ref=cloudanix.com)
4. [AWS Trusted Advisor](https://aws.amazon.com/premiumsupport/technology/trusted-advisor/?ref=cloudanix.com)
5. [Amazon Cloudwatch](https://aws.amazon.com/cloudwatch/?ref=cloudanix.com)


Now I will briefly explain each of the above tools work and how they can help you with cost management in AWS bills.


## Billing and Cost Management Tool


The Amazon Console billing section gives access to all your activities, including what services you are consuming on AWS. It helps you optimize your usage structure so you can manage AWS effectively and reduce your cost if appropriately used. You must use tagging to organize services by project or department. This tool lets you merge AWS accounts and create a single billing entity for each project’s separate budget. Getting this right depends on solid[cloud asset management](https://www.cloudanix.com/learn/what-is-cloud-asset-management) — an accurate[cloud inventory](https://www.cloudanix.com/cloud-inventory) is what lets tags map cleanly onto what you actually run across accounts.


### AWS Cost Explorer


This tool gives you an overview of usage, costs, and returns on investment for AWS. It shows you data for the past 13 months of AWS usage and predicts your future expenditure. This tool also helps you to create customized views to help analyze costs and identify areas for improvement of your AWS bills.


It also provides you with an API so you can access the data via your analytics tool.


> **2026 update — Cost Explorer now looks back further and has better commitment recommendations.** Cost Explorer’s historical range has been extended (you can analyze up to **38 months** of history, not just 13), which makes year-over-year trend analysis realistic. It also includes built-in **Savings Plans and Reserved Instance recommendations** that tell you the specific commitment to buy and the estimated saving. Two related modern points: for large-scale or programmatic analysis, AWS now offers **Data Exports** (which superseded the older Cost and Usage Report workflow) to push detailed billing data into Amazon S3 for querying in Athena or your BI tool; and the free “hourly + resource-level” granularity in Cost Explorer must be explicitly enabled and carries a small charge, so turn it on only when you need that depth.


### AWS Budgets


This tool lets you set and enforce the budget for specific services and receive notifications in the form of emails or messages from Simple Notification Services (SNS) when the budget reaches or exceeds the set limit. We can specify an overall cost budget and even set it to specific data points, such as several instances per data usage. The dashboard of AWS Budgets provides similar views to those of AWS Cost Explorer, showing how services are being used according to the set budget and how you can optimize your AWS bills.


> **2026 update — Budgets can now take action, not just notify.** The most useful evolution here is **AWS Budget Actions** : when a budget threshold is crossed, Budgets can automatically apply an IAM or Service Control Policy, or stop/downscale targeted EC2 or RDS instances — so a runaway environment can be throttled without waiting for a human to read the email. You can also create **budgets from templates** (for example, a “zero spend” budget to catch any charge on an account that should be free-tier only) in a couple of clicks. A common 2026 setup pairs Budgets (fixed guardrails and automated actions) with Cost Anomaly Detection (adaptive, ML-based alerts) so you catch both “we exceeded the number we set” and “something is behaving abnormally that we did not anticipate.”


### AWS Trusted Advisor


It is a tool that provides guidance based on specific services in AWS. Trusted Advisor checks these five areas, and one of those includes cost optimization. It offers automated optimization recommendations related to:


> **2026 update — Trusted Advisor now covers more than five areas, and its cost checks are no longer the best place to start for cost optimization.** Trusted Advisor’s check categories have expanded beyond the original five to include **Cost Optimization, Performance, Security, Fault Tolerance (Resilience), Service Limits (Service Quotas), and Operational Excellence** . Two practical points for 2026: first, the deepest Trusted Advisor checks require a Business, Enterprise On-Ramp, or Enterprise Support plan (the free tier exposes only a limited subset), so confirm your support level before relying on it. Second, for *cost* specifically, AWS now steers you to the dedicated **Cost Optimization Hub** (described in the note below) rather than Trusted Advisor’s cost checks, because the Hub consolidates far more recommendation types with quantified savings. Use Trusted Advisor for its broader operational, security, and resilience checks, and use Cost Optimization Hub as your primary cost-savings tool. The specific cost recommendations listed below are still valid examples of what to look for.


1. Underutilized EBS volumes
2. Unassociated elastic IP addresses
3. Idle load balancers
4. Idle Database instances on Amazon RDS
5. Load utilization of EC2 instances
6. Redundant route 53 latency resource record sets
7. EC2 reserved instance optimization and lease expiration
8. Underutilized Amazon Redshift clusters


### Amazon Cloudwatch


It lets you set alarms based on a variety of metrics captured from your AWS usage. It is used for AWS bills optimization, and you can set limits as to when you want to be alarmed. This way you are having strict rules set for your AWS Bills strategy!


> **2026 addition — three free AWS cost tools that did not exist when this article was written, and that you should add to the list above.**
>
>
> - **Cost Optimization Hub** (launched at re:Invent 2023, free). This is now the single best starting point for saving money. It consolidates 18+ types of recommendations — EC2 rightsizing, idle-resource detection, Graviton migration, and Reserved Instance/Savings Plans purchase suggestions — across **all your accounts and Regions in one place** , each with an estimated dollar saving, and it deduplicates overlapping advice so you are not double-counting. If you read only one tool in your account after this article, make it this one.
> - **AWS Cost Anomaly Detection** (free). This uses machine learning to learn your normal spend patterns and alerts you when spend deviates — for example, a runaway job or a misconfigured resource driving an unexpected spike. It is more intelligent than the fixed thresholds of AWS Budgets because it adapts to your baseline, and it is the modern answer to “how do I find out about a surprise bill *before* the end of the month?”
> - **AWS Compute Optimizer** (free). It analyzes actual utilization and recommends right-sized EC2 instances, EBS volumes, Lambda memory settings, and more, so you stop paying for capacity you never use. Its savings estimates line up with Cost Optimization Hub.
>
>
> The 2020-era workflow in this article (Cost Explorer + Budgets + CloudWatch + Trusted Advisor) is still valid, but in 2026 the efficient path is: **Cost Optimization Hub** to find savings, **Compute Optimizer** to right-size, **Savings Plans** to lock in commitment discounts, **Cost Anomaly Detection** to catch surprises, and **Cost Explorer/Budgets** for reporting and guardrails. Tagging everything with **cost allocation tags** remains the foundation that makes all of these tools useful.
